title: Denkyira: The Kingdom of Gold and Pride

pages.text: Stand on the bridge at Dunkwa and look down at the River Offin. For as long as anyone can remember, people have washed gold from its sands and dug it from the land around. Today the river often runs brown with mud from illegal mining. Three hundred and fifty years ago, the gold of this same valley belonged to one kingdom. Its name was Denkyira. Its king had so much gold that, people said, he never used the same ornaments twice. For a time it ruled most of the forest country. Then, in a single afternoon, it lost everything.
sentences: Stand on the bridge at Dunkwa and look down at the River Offin.

Today the river often runs brown with mud from illegal mining.
Three hundred and fifty years ago, the gold of this same valley belonged to one kingdom.
Its name was Denkyira.
Its king had so much gold that, people said, he never used the same ornaments twice.
For a time it ruled most of the forest country.
Then, in a single afternoon, it lost everything.
pages.alt: A wide brown river under a bridge, with forested banks and a town beyond.

pages.text: Denkyira was an Akan state. Its capital, Abankeseso, lay in the forest near the Offin. In the 1600s, its kings defeated their neighbours one by one, beginning with the old state of Adansi. They took control of the richest gold fields and of the trade paths that led to the European forts on the coast, where gold was exchanged for guns and cloth. With guns, they won more wars. The greatest of these kings was Boa Amponsem. Under him, almost every state in the central forest paid tribute to Denkyira.

Its capital, Abankeseso, lay in the forest near the Offin.
In the 1600s, its kings defeated their neighbours one by one, beginning with the old state of Adansi.
They took control of the richest gold fields and of the trade paths that led to the European forts on the coast, where gold was exchanged for guns and cloth.
With guns, they won more wars.
The greatest of these kings was Boa Amponsem.
Under him, almost every state in the central forest paid tribute to Denkyira.
pages.alt: A forest town with a large royal courtyard, with porters arriving carrying loads on their heads.

pages.text: Tribute was the price of defeat. Each year, the weaker states had to send gold, food, and people to Abankeseso. They also had to send young royals to live at the court of Denkyira. This was meant to keep their families obedient. One of these young men came from Kwaman, a small state in the north. He served at court and watched closely how a powerful kingdom was governed and how its army was organised. His name was Osei Tutu. Denkyira had taken him in to keep his people weak. In fact, it was training its own conqueror.

pages.text: When Boa Amponsem died, a young king named Ntim Gyakari came to the stool. The stories say that he was proud and hasty. He demanded far more from the tribute states than before. Tradition tells that he sent a great brass basin to the Asante chiefs and ordered them to fill it with gold dust, and to send their favourite wives and children as well. By then the Asante states had united around the Golden Stool. They refused. One chief is said to have filled the basin with stones. It was an insult, and it meant war.

pages.alt: A large brass basin set down before a circle of chiefs, one of whom is rising angrily to his feet.

pages.text: The armies met at Feyiase, near Kumasi, around 1701. Denkyira was richer and had more guns. But many of its subject states had been waiting for this moment and went over to the Asante side. The Denkyira army was broken. Tradition says that Ntim Gyakari was found sitting in his camp, wearing golden ornaments and playing a board game, certain that he could not lose. He was killed there. The richest king in the forest had fallen in a day. Asante took Denkyira’s gold, its trade paths, and its place as the leading power of the forest.

pages.text: Denkyira did not disappear. Its people later moved south, and their king has his seats at Dunkwa-on-Offin and at Jukwa, near Cape Coast. But the kingdom never ruled the forest again. Its story is told all over Ghana as a warning. Wealth and weapons made Denkyira strong, and pride made it careless. It pressed its neighbours so hard that they united against it. The gold is still in the Offin valley, and so is the lesson: riches taken without care for others, or for the land, can ruin those who take them.

activities.question: What made Denkyira so powerful in the 1600s?
options: It controlled rich gold fields and the trade paths to the coast
It had the largest fishing fleet
It was protected by the British

activities.question: Why did Denkyira keep young royals from other states at its court?
Why did Denkyira lose at Feyiase even though it was richer?
options: Many of its subject states joined the Asante side
Its king was away at the coast

activities.question: Apply it: A company makes large profits by polluting the river that a town depends on. Which lesson from Denkyira applies?
options: Wealth gained without care for others can bring ruin
Gold should be left in the ground for ever

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Denkyira defeats Adansi and takes the gold fields
Boa Amponsem rules and most forest states pay tribute
Osei Tutu serves at the court of Denkyira
Ntim Gyakari demands a basin of gold
